definition.text: Running a business so that it makes money while keeping its harm to the environment, local communities and society as small as possible.

facts.text: Such firms aim at the triple bottom line of profit, people and planet, weighing environmental, economic and social factors in their decisions.
A green business offers products that cut demand for harmful ones, keeps its finances sound, respects human rights and supports inclusion of local and global communities.
The idea grew out of late-20th-century debates on sustainable development; the 1987 report Our Common Future shaped how private firms thought about managing the environment.
A central aim is to cut the environmental harm from making and using goods, for example by measuring carbon footprints, cutting waste and redesigning products to last longer.
The business historian Geoffrey Jones traces green business back to start-ups in organic food and wind and solar energy before World War 1.
If a firm's whole model is unsustainable, becoming sustainable can mean rebuilding it, for example moving from selling cars to offering car sharing.
Firms often meet only the lowest standards; real sustainability is said to need a purpose that goes beyond legal compliance.

title: Corporate environmental responsibility

definition.text: A company's duty to avoid damaging the natural environment.

facts.text: The term comes from corporate social responsibility (CSR); CER deals strictly with environmental effects inside company strategy, while CSR leans toward social matters.
Protecting the environment used to be seen as the government's job, done through rules and penalties; the private sector has since taken on a shared responsibility.
Its main elements are using resources efficiently and limiting activities that would spoil resources for future generations.
Its main drivers are government policies and rules, backed by subsidies, tariffs and taxes, plus pressure from media, the public, shareholders and NGOs.
Obstacles include the cost of regulation, uncertain economic gains, expensive new technology and rules that differ from country to country.
It is unclear which emissions a firm answers for when they are spread across suppliers and outsourcing, or whether it should answer for past emissions made before the harm was known.
Stakeholders' growing awareness of how much harm business does to the environment has made it more institutionalized.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether firms must go beyond the law or should first make profits for shareholders, and on which emissions a firm is responsible for.

definition.text: Plans a company uses to win new revenue from sustainability while guarding against rising energy, regulation and resource costs and shifting customer views.

facts.text: Common strategies are innovation, collaboration, process improvement and sustainability reporting, plus greening the supply chain.
The Sustainability Balanced Scorecard measures performance by balancing financial and non-financial, short- and long-term goals, building environmental and social aims into management.
A 2023 Swiss survey of 514 small and medium firms found 89% had never produced a sustainability report.

definition.text: A business's responsibility for the well-being of its employees, customers and community.

facts.text: Firms contribute by supporting education, encouraging staff to volunteer and giving to charity.
It is often tied to environmental justice: social fairness and environmental care affect each other.

title: Sustainability and financial performance

definition.text: The debate over whether a company's environmental and social efforts raise or lower its profits.

facts.text: A positive link between environmental performance and economic performance has been reported.
A 2026 study of Indian firms found that steady improvement in environmental performance went with better financial results.
A 2023 study of European listed firms found the opposite of a 'win-win': stronger sustainability practices went with lower profitability, at least for a time.
Studies link sustainability practices to financial success and customer satisfaction, but mostly at larger firms with more money to spend on them.
Gains can include attracting staff, tax breaks and new markets.

contested_note: Some studies find sustainability raises financial performance while a 2023 study of European firms found it lowered profitability.
notes: Passes test 5: discussed on Sustainable business, Corporate environmental responsibility and Corporate social responsibility (see part02).

title: Strategic support for environmental regulation
article: Corporate environmental responsibility#Benefits of corporate environmental responsibility

definition.text: A firm backing new environmental rules because they will hurt its competitors more than itself.

facts.text: Many firms find it pays to argue for environmental rules and prepare for them before they become law.
One study found firms support climate laws to gain power over competitors, accepting short-term costs to come out ahead in the long run.

definition.text: A design approach that cuts a product's or service's harm to health and the environment, counting impacts across its whole life cycle.

facts.text: Its four parts are cleaner processing and manufacturing, greener packaging, design for disposal or reuse, and energy efficiency.
Life-cycle assessment is used to compare design options and pick the least harmful.
Claimed benefits are cost savings, lower risk, new market openings and meeting regulations.
Sustainable business leaders treat it as part of their work, along with counting life-cycle costs.

title: Corporate social responsibility

definition.text: Companies running their main business responsibly and sustainably so that their overall effect on society is positive.

facts.text: It is a form of private business self-regulation that aims to help social and environmental goals by reducing harm, such as cutting a firm's carbon footprint.
Since the 1960s it has gone by many names, including corporate sustainability, sustainable business, corporate citizenship and responsible business, and there is little agreement on a definition.
A business person may see it as strategy, an NGO activist as greenwash and a government official as voluntary regulation.
Howard Bowen's 1953 book Social Responsibilities of the Businessman is widely seen as the founding work; he argued business leaders' duties go beyond making profit.
Firms take it up for strategic, ethical or instrumental reasons; for listed companies it often takes the form of ESG practices and reports.
It has been shifting from voluntary choices by single firms toward mandatory schemes at regional, national and international levels.
Its scope widened from a firm's own conduct to its suppliers, how its products are used and how they are thrown away.
Supporters say it raises long-term profits; critics say it distracts from a firm's economic role or is mere window-dressing.

contested_note: Supporters argue CSR raises long-term profits, while critics say it distracts from business's economic role or is window-dressing.

title: Stakeholder theory

definition.text: The view that a firm is answerable not only to its shareholders but to every group with a relationship to it, such as workers, customers, suppliers and communities.

facts.text: The word stakeholder was coined in English by Eric Rhenman in his 1968 book Industrial Democracy and Industrial Management; R. Edward Freeman later developed the theory.
A review of 14,523 articles found the stakeholder view to be the most common dimension of CSR.
One reason firms adopt CSR is to satisfy stakeholders beyond their shareholders.
The EU defines CSR as a firm being accountable for its impact on all relevant stakeholders.
Critics say the stakeholder view ignores how complex the networks in cross-sector partnerships are.

notes: No crawled page of its own; passes test 5 (stakeholders discussed on Corporate social responsibility, Corporate environmental responsibility and Sustainable business). Suggested page: Stakeholder theory.

definition.text: Archie Carroll's four-part framework of what society expects of business: economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities.

facts.text: Carroll began developing it after his 1979 Academy of Management Review article on corporate social performance.
It is often drawn as a pyramid of responsibilities: economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic.

title: Shareholder value versus social responsibility

definition.text: The argument over whether a company exists only to earn returns for its owners within the law, or also owes duties to society and the environment.

facts.text: Milton Friedman argued a firm's purpose is to maximize returns to shareholders, and that obeying the law is socially responsible enough.
Friedman said people may spend their own money on causes, but owners should not raise prices to fund social goals unrelated to profit, which he likened to a tax on consumers.
In the 1930s Berle and Dodd debated whether directors should be bound by enforceable rules to serve labour, customers and the public as well as shareholders.
Some argue better government regulation is the alternative to voluntary CSR; others reply that mandated programs distort how resources are allocated.
Some studies find CSR serves managers' interests at shareholders' cost, a kind of agency problem.

contested_note: Friedman and others hold that a firm's only duty is profit within the law, while CSR supporters argue firms owe wider duties to society.

title: Social license to operate
article: Corporate social responsibility#Social license to operate

definition.text: The ongoing support and approval that local communities and other stakeholders give to a company's activities.

facts.text: The term was introduced in 1997 and has been used mostly in resource extraction industries to describe company-community relations.
Without it, local people may block projects, staff may leave and firms may face ongoing legal challenges.
It is granted by communities, not governments, and can take a long time to win but be lost very quickly.
It rests on relationships and trust; local firms tend to gain it more easily than outside ones.
Showing commitment to CSR is one way to earn it, by improving a firm's reputation.

verification.title: Social license to operate: Legitimacy by another name?

definition.text: Six kinds of activity through which companies practise CSR, from donations to behaviour-change campaigns.

facts.text: They are corporate philanthropy, community volunteering, socially responsible business practices, cause promotion, cause-related marketing and corporate social marketing.
Philanthropy and volunteering usually have no profit motive; the rest can be cause marketing, which pursues both profit and social good.

title: Social accounting
article: Corporate social responsibility#Accounting, auditing, and reporting

definition.text: Reporting the social and environmental effects of a company's economic activity to interest groups and to society at large.

facts.text: It stresses that corporations should be accountable for their effects.
There is no single fixed standard; frameworks include AA1000, based on the triple bottom line, the Global Reporting Initiative guidelines and ISO 14000.

title: Socially responsible investing

definition.text: Investors using where they put their money to encourage company behaviour they consider responsible.

facts.text: What counts as ethical varies: some religious investors withdraw money from firms that offend their views, while secular investors divest from firms imposing religious views.

notes: May duplicate an investing entry in the finance-for-conservation chapter.

title: CSR as misdirection

definition.text: The criticism that companies use social responsibility programs to draw attention away from harmful parts of their business.

facts.text: Unproven social claims and outright greenwashing have made consumers more cynical and distrustful.
The tobacco industry funded research in genetics, viruses and air pollution, which drew attention from the link between smoking and cancer.
US firms convicted of bribery got more lenient fines if they were seen to engage in CSR: a 20% rise in corporate giving went with a 40% lower fine.
A review of 700 sources found firms engage in CSR mainly for expected financial gain rather than a wish to serve society.

contested_note: Critics see CSR as a distraction from harmful practices, while supporters see it as genuine responsibility.

title: Resource-based view of CSR

definition.text: A way of judging the costs and benefits of CSR by asking whether it gives a firm a competitive advantage that rivals cannot copy.

facts.text: Barney (1990) held that lasting advantage needs resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable.
Reinhardt (1998) found a CSR-based strategy earns above-normal returns only if competitors cannot imitate it.
McWilliams and Siegel argued managers can set CSR spending through cost-benefit analysis like any other investment.
Waddock and Graves (1997) linked social and financial performance; McWilliams and Siegel (2000) said innovation, not CSR, drove the gains.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on whether CSR itself or innovation explains the link between social and financial performance.

definition.text: Choosing what to buy, and what to boycott, according to how products affect people, animals and the environment.

facts.text: It is a form of consumer activism based on 'dollar voting'.
Its rise over the last two decades is linked to the rise of CSR.
Criteria-based ethical and environmental ratings of companies, first used for shoppers, are now common in business sustainability ratings, and ESG ratings reach stock traders' screens.
More consumers demand sustainable goods, especially when they think firms neglect the environment.
Its growth is held back by routine buying that leaves no room for reflection and by competing moral demands in daily life.

definition.text: The gap between consumers saying they will buy only from responsible companies and what they actually buy.

facts.text: Many consumers want to buy from responsible firms, yet ethical purchases are a small share of household spending.
One explanation is the bystander effect: people act less when others seem not to care.
Another is that ethical products cost more but give the buyer little extra in return.
A Lisbon study found price, limited access and lack of education held back less engaged shoppers of sustainable fashion.

title: Nature-positive

definition.text: A goal to halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030 and to achieve its full recovery by 2050.

facts.text: Progress is measured against a baseline of biodiversity in 2020.
It matches the 2030 mission and 2050 vision of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, though the framework does not name it.
It was proposed as a single global goal for nature to sit beside climate and development goals, aiming at an 'Equitable, Nature-Positive, Carbon Neutral world'.
Unlike earlier approaches, it covers a company's whole value chain, not just direct impacts, and aims for absolute rather than relative gains.
Over 90 world leaders signed the Leaders' Pledge for Nature, and the G7 committed to it at its 2021 summit.
Critics call it vague and open to greenwashing, and warn of the 'financialization of nature'.
To avoid greenwashing, Milner-Gulland proposed it needs a measured baseline, timeframe, target, clear actions, regular monitoring and disclosure.
Its 'net' approach is criticised for implying continued loss and assuming like-for-like compensation is possible.

contested_note: Critics call nature-positive vague, open to greenwashing and a route to financializing nature, while its proponents say business must be part of the solution.

title: Mainstreaming nature in business

definition.text: Building nature into a company's decision-making, governance, strategy and risk management rather than leaving it to site ecologists.

facts.text: It sets the nature-positive approach apart from no net loss and net positive impact, where biodiversity is handled by ecological managers at project sites.
Since the Kunming-Montreal framework began, nature-positive has helped mainstream nature through businesses and governance systems.

notes: No page of its own; passes test 5 (Nature-positive and Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework). May duplicate a biodiversity mainstreaming entry elsewhere.

definition.text: Managing the environmental, social and economic effects of goods and services, and encouraging good governance, across their whole life cycle from suppliers to customers.

facts.text: Traditional supply chain goals were lower costs, just-in-time delivery and faster transport; rising environmental and social costs and consumer pressure added sustainability as a new measure.
Many firms can measure only their own operations, not their suppliers' and customers', which makes their true environmental and social costs hard to know.
Depending on industry and position, suppliers can account for most of a company's total emissions.
Buyers use their purchasing power to set standards for suppliers, treating sustainability like cost, quality and timeliness.
Tools include supplier scorecards, life-cycle assessments, surveys and rewards for suppliers that improve.
A 2017 study found suppliers farther upstream, away from the end user, had the most to gain financially from sustainable supply chain management.
After the COVID-19 disruptions, sustainable supply chains proved more resilient, with lower supplier risk.
A 2020 Boston Consulting Group survey found 70% of consumers willing to pay a 5% premium for more sustainably made products.

definition.text: Visits to supplier sites to check that they meet social and environmental standards.

facts.text: Audits can certify a supplier against an outside standard such as SA8000 or ISO 14001, or against a buyer's own supplier code of conduct.
Buyers may audit suppliers themselves or send third-party auditors.
Buyers often deal with only one tier of suppliers, while their supply chain stretches through many tiers upstream.

title: Supply chain transparency

definition.text: Making it possible to see and trace where goods come from and how they were made along the supply chain.

facts.text: Consumers increasingly demand transparency and traceability, especially where forced or child labour is involved in traded goods.
Forced labour often happens upstream, where buyers and end users can see little.
Transparent supply chains matter for global goals such as ending net deforestation.
Transparency shapes how consumers view and support companies.

notes: No page of its own; passes test 5 (Supply chain sustainability and Sustainable consumption).

title: Scope 3 emissions

definition.text: The indirect greenhouse gas emissions in a company's value chain, such as those of its suppliers and from the use of its products.

facts.text: Scope 1 covers a firm's direct emissions from its own facilities, and Scope 2 the emissions from energy it buys.
Scope 3 emissions are especially hard to estimate.
In 2020, 81% of S&P 500 companies reported Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions.
The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive requires large and listed firms to disclose material Scope 3 emissions, starting with 2025 reports on 2024 data.
The US SEC's 2024 rule requires Scope 3 reporting if emissions are material or part of corporate targets, though the regulator has signalled it may change this.
In 2021, 61% of Chevron shareholders backed a resolution asking it to cut emissions including Scope 3.

notes: No page of its own; defined in Carbon accounting lead and used on Supply chain sustainability, Science Based Targets initiative, Business action on climate change and BSI PAS 2060 (test 5). Suggested page: Greenhouse Gas Protocol.

title: Double materiality

definition.text: The principle that a company should report both how sustainability issues affect its finances and how it affects society and the environment.

facts.text: Some supply chain impacts are doubly material: the firm harms the environment, and the same issues bring risks or opportunities for the firm.
The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive uses a double materiality test covering impacts on the company and on the public.
The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive uses a double materiality test, covering impacts on both the company and the public.
The Global Reporting Initiative's standards focus on impact materiality, while the European reporting standards focus on double materiality.

notes: No page of its own; passes test 5 (Supply chain sustainability, Carbon accounting, Global Reporting Initiative). Likely also drafted from Sustainability reporting (chunk 05).

title: Science-based emissions targets

definition.text: Company targets for cutting greenhouse gas emissions that are set in line with climate science and the Paris Agreement goals.

facts.text: The Science Based Targets initiative, set up in 2015, helps companies set such targets and validates them.
As of 2025, over 10,000 companies had set or committed to setting targets validated by the SBTi.
In October 2021 the SBTi launched the first net zero standard, for targets consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 °C.
Best practice includes transition plans covering scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, short-term milestones, board oversight and executive pay linked to milestones.
The SBTi says residual emissions in most sectors should fall below 10% of an organization's baseline by 2050.
A 2024 plan to let companies use environmental attribute certificates against Scope 3 targets drew protest from SBTi staff, who argued offsets are incompatible with the Paris Agreement.

contested_note: Whether companies may count carbon offsets or certificates toward science-based targets is disputed, including within the SBTi.
notes: The organisation itself (an NGO) gets no entry per the brief; this entry teaches the target-setting method, using its page as the canonical article.

title: Insetting
article: Science Based Targets initiative#Carbon offsets controversy

definition.text: A business-coined way for a company to claim it has met emission targets by means other than cutting its own emissions.

facts.text: The SBTi's forestry, land and agriculture guidance of September 2022 allows insetting, breaking with its long-held view that targets be met only by emission cuts.
The term was created by the private sector and is not defined in international standards such as ISO 14050 or the IWA 42 Net Zero Guidelines.

title: Business action on climate change

definition.text: What businesses do about climate change, from cutting their own emissions to trying to influence climate regulation such as the Kyoto Protocol.

facts.text: Business helps mitigation by investing in new energy technologies and energy efficiency.
Firms act to improve their image, align with owners, staff, suppliers and customers, cut costs and reduce exposure to costs they cannot control.
Energy efficiency often pays off only in the medium to long term while shareholders want short-term results, so regulation is often needed.
Many firms that once denied climate change, including major oil and car companies, changed position as scientific and political consensus grew.
By 2007 the Carbon Disclosure Project published emissions data for 2400 of the largest corporations, backed by investors with $41 trillion in assets.
Small and medium enterprises account for around 13% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Physical risks of climate change top the list of business concerns for US and EU firms.
A 2025 PwC report found 84% of companies keeping or speeding up their climate targets.

notes: Most of the page is company-by-company detail (BP, ExxonMobil, Shell, banks), which was left out.

title: Corporate climate denial lobbying

definition.text: Efforts by large companies, mainly in the United States, to block climate regulation through lobbying and by funding people who deny climate change.

facts.text: In 1989 US oil and car industries formed the Global Climate Coalition to oppose mandatory action on global warming; it dissolved itself in 2002.
The coalition paid credentialed deniers as spokespeople and fought the Kyoto Protocol, while its own experts said the greenhouse science could not be refuted.
In 1997 industry funded a $13 million advertising campaign before the US Senate voted against ratifying the Kyoto Protocol.
A 1998 American Petroleum Institute memo set out a plan to make uncertainty about climate science part of conventional wisdom.

notes: No section of its own outside organisation pages; passes test 5 (Business action on climate change and the Global Climate Coalition page). The coalition itself gets no entry.

title: Carbon bomb
article: List of locations and entities by greenhouse gas emissions#Carbon bomb projects (new extractions)

definition.text: A new fossil fuel extraction project whose potential emissions exceed 1 billion tonnes of CO2.

facts.text: A 2022 study counted 425 such coal, oil and gas projects worldwide; their potential emissions are twice the Paris Agreement's 1.5 °C carbon budget.
Studies say large amounts of fossil fuel must stay in the ground for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5 °C.
The researchers argue 'defusing' carbon bombs should be a priority for climate policy.

verification.title: “Carbon Bombs” - Mapping key fossil fuel projects
verification.evidence: We list these “carbon bombs” by name, show in which countries they are located and calculate their potential emissions which combined exceed the global 1.5 °C carbon budget by a factor of two.

sources.title: List of locations and entities by greenhouse gas emissions
sources.key: List of locations and entities by greenhouse gas emissions

title: Corporate sustainability

definition.text: A business approach that aims to create long-term value for stakeholders by building ethical, social, environmental, cultural and economic concerns into company strategy.

facts.text: It is often confused with corporate social responsibility, but scholars say the key difference is time: sustainability asks firms to make trade-offs across time to protect future generations.
The idea grew out of sustainable development, as defined by the Brundtland Commission, and John Elkington's 1997 'triple bottom line'.
In the research literature it is usually treated as a three-part idea combining social, environmental and economic factors.
Its most widely accepted test is whether a firm uses natural capital efficiently, including keeping vital ecosystem services such as climate regulation and water purification.
Firms often state their commitment through Corporate Sustainability Standards, policies meant to meet or go beyond minimum legal requirements.
Whether it can be measured is disputed, because there is no generally accepted set of indicators separating sustainable from unsustainable operation.
Short-term thinking is described as the main enemy of corporate sustainability.

contested_note: Sources say it remains contested whether corporate sustainability can be measured at all.

definition.text: Eco-efficiency compares the economic value a firm adds with its total ecological impact; socio-efficiency compares that value with the firm's social impact.

facts.text: Most corporate effects on the environment are assumed to be negative, while social effects can be positive, such as job creation, or negative, such as work accidents.
Both measures mainly aim at economic sustainability, treating natural and social capital as tools for win-win gains.
Some authors argue sustainable development instead needs eco-effectiveness, socio-effectiveness, sufficiency and eco-equity.

title: Creating shared value

definition.text: A business strategy in which a company seeks profit by solving social problems linked to its own operations, improving its competitiveness and the conditions of its communities at once.

facts.text: Michael Porter and Mark Kramer introduced the idea in a 2006 Harvard Business Review article and expanded it in a January 2011 follow-up.
Companies can create shared value in three ways: reconceiving products and markets, redefining productivity in the value chain, and enabling local cluster development.
Kramer says the main difference from corporate social responsibility is that CSR is about responsibility, while shared value is about creating value.
Accounting for ecological costs is hard: up to 90% of the ecological footprint in food processing comes from land management outside corporations' control.
Counting ecosystem services at the farm level lets shared value include positive environmental externalities in the economic system.
Reviewers found little rigorous analysis of its impact; most evidence comes from standalone case studies of mixed quality.
The Economist called the concept 'undercooked', and a common criticism is that it plays down the trade-offs businesses must make.
Critics have noted its 'striking resemblance' to Jed Emerson's earlier idea of blended value.

contested_note: Porter presents shared value as a win-win, while critics such as The Economist call it undercooked and say it ignores trade-offs.

title: Bottom of the pyramid and inclusive business

definition.text: Inclusive business models create value by selling products and services to the poor or buying from them, bringing poor people directly into companies' value chains.

facts.text: Shared value work has focused on the 'bottom of the pyramid' because this group has greater social needs and offers new markets.
Prahalad and Hart's paper 'The Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid' argued that serving poor consumers offers both commercial and social opportunities.
A classic example is Hindustan Unilever selling hygiene products in smaller package sizes suited to poor customers.
In an IFC survey, around 90% of 167 applicants named access to finance as a main obstacle to inclusive business models.

title: EU taxonomy for sustainable activities

definition.text: A European Union classification system that defines which economic activities count as environmentally sustainable, created under the European Green Deal.

facts.text: Its aim is to prevent greenwashing and help investors make informed sustainable investment decisions.
It covers six environmental objectives: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, circular economy, pollution prevention, water and marine resources, and biodiversity and ecosystems.
The Taxonomy came into force in July 2020 as part of the European Green Deal, which aims for a carbon neutral economy by 2050.
A Technical Expert Group set up in 2018 developed the technical screening criteria used to judge whether an activity is sustainable.
The Environmental Delegated Act, published on 21 November 2023, set criteria for the remaining objectives, including protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
Banks must disclose a 'green asset ratio'; early estimates put the EU banks' average at 2.23%.
An EU green bond standard under development would require issuers to fund activities aligned with the taxonomy.

notes: EU-wide regulation (Regulation 2020/852); kept as a multi-country framework seeded in this chapter.

title: Do no significant harm

definition.text: The rule that an activity counts as sustainable under the EU taxonomy only if it contributes substantially to one environmental objective without seriously harming any of the other five.

facts.text: An activity must meet four requirements: a substantial contribution to one objective, no significant harm to the others, minimum social safeguards, and the technical screening criteria.
The Technical Expert Group held back from including nuclear energy because it could not settle whether nuclear met this principle.

distinct_from: Natural gas and nuclear in the EU taxonomy

title: Natural gas and nuclear in the EU taxonomy
article: EU taxonomy for sustainable activities#Debate over natural gas and nuclear energy

definition.text: The dispute over whether fossil gas and nuclear power should be labelled as environmentally sustainable investments under the EU taxonomy.

facts.text: The Complementary Climate Delegated Act, the most controversial one, listed certain gas and nuclear activities as transitional activities that help mitigate climate change.
Expert advice split: the Technical Expert Group did not recommend including nuclear, while the Joint Research Centre found its impact would stay below harmful levels.
Some countries see gas as a bridge from coal to renewables, while the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden and Denmark opposed including it.
On 6 July 2022 a resolution to reject the act failed in the European Parliament: 278 MEPs backed it when 353 votes were needed.

contested_note: Member states, expert bodies and industry groups disagree on whether gas and nuclear power are sustainable.

title: Environmental audit

definition.text: An evaluation that finds gaps in an organization's compliance with environmental rules and in its environmental management system, and sets out corrective actions.

facts.text: Environmental audits do for environmental performance what financial audits do for accounts.
There are two main types: compliance audits and management system audits.
Compliance audits check a site against the laws, regulations, permits and local codes that apply to it.
A multimedia audit covers all environmental media such as air, water and waste; a programmatic audit covers only chosen areas, such as air.
ISO 14001 certification does not by itself prove legal compliance, though the standard requires firms to evaluate their compliance.
Auditors work from a checklist called a protocol, and there is no standard protocol in form or content.
Professionals have long debated detailed, prescriptive protocols against flexible ones that rely on auditor expertise.
Satellite imagery and geographic information systems are an emerging audit technology.

contested_note: Audit professionals disagree on whether detailed prescriptive protocols or flexible expert-led ones work better.

definition.text: A system of policies, procedures and processes that a firm uses to train staff and to monitor, summarize and report its environmental performance to people inside and outside the firm.

facts.text: The most widely used standard for an EMS is ISO 14001, part of the ISO 14000 family first developed in March 1996.
Its goals are to increase compliance with legal standards and to reduce waste, going beyond compliance to cut environmental impact.
An EMS meeting ISO 14001 helps an organization identify and control its environmental impacts, improve its performance continually, and set and track objectives.
It follows a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, a process of continual improvement in which the system is constantly reviewed and revised.
The model can be used by organizations ranging from factories to service industries to government agencies.
Organizations usually seek certification from independent bodies, which confirm the EMS conforms to ISO 14001.
An EMS also encourages contractors and suppliers to set up their own systems.

definition.text: A management tool that traces the physical flows of materials and energy through a company or supply chain and assigns costs to them, to reveal and reduce their environmental and financial costs.

facts.text: Its aim is to improve both environmental and economic performance through better use of materials and energy.
Developed in Germany in the 1980s, it became very successful in Japan, where up to 300 companies had used it by 2010.
In 2011 the International Organization for Standardization published a standard for it, ISO 14051.
It was developed in Germany in the 1980s and became a huge success in Japan in the 2000s.

definition.text: The disclosure, voluntary or required, of a company's non-financial performance information to people outside the organization.

facts.text: It covers environmental, social, economic and governance issues, the criteria grouped under the acronym ESG.
It goes by many names, including ESG reporting, non-financial reporting, CSR reporting and social reporting.
It grew from environmental reporting, which became popular in the 1970s, and has expanded greatly over the last twenty years.
It rests on the stakeholder model: following Freeman, employees, customers, suppliers, communities and governments matter as well as shareholders.
Its growth was driven by awareness of the ecological crisis and by corporate scandals such as Enron and the 2008 financial crisis.
The Global Reporting Initiative standards are the most widely used benchmark for sustainability reports worldwide.
Critics say the many competing frameworks make reports hard to compare, undermining transparency.
Some firms manipulate reports by hiding negative or over-stating positive environmental data, a practice linked to greenwashing.

title: Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive

definition.text: The European Union law that sets uniform sustainability reporting rules for companies, replacing the earlier Non-Financial Reporting Directive.

facts.text: It was adopted in December 2022, came into force on 5 January 2023, and applies in stages from 1 January 2024.
It widened reporting to about 50.000 organizations in Europe, against roughly 11,600 companies covered by the older directive by 2021.
Companies exceeding two of three thresholds must report: 250 employees, a €25 million balance sheet, or €50 million net turnover.
In February 2025 the Commission proposed an 'Omnibus' simplification package and a two-year delay, to 2028, for later waves of companies.

notes: EU-wide law, kept because it sets the reporting rules for tens of thousands of firms; 50.000 is the source's own notation.

definition.text: Obtaining the materials, products and services a company needs from suppliers in a way that is socially and environmentally responsible while still economically sound.

facts.text: Global supply chains and pressure to cut costs have harmed environments and communities, especially in developing nations, and awareness has grown since the 1990s.
A company is understood to be only as sustainable as the start of its supply chain.
Supply chains harm nature mainly through resource depletion and pollution, leading to biodiversity loss, habitat destruction and soil degradation.
Firms put it into practice through supplier codes of conduct, supplier selection and assessment, and supplier development.
It grew out of corporate social responsibility, which took on environmental duties in the 1990s with Elkington's triple bottom line.
Responsible sourcing means complying with ethical rules such as no child labour; sustainable sourcing goes further and acts to improve conditions.
The growing number of standards has raised costs for producers and caused confusion over their meaning and legitimacy.
It relates directly to Sustainable Development Goal 12, responsible consumption and production.

definition.text: Requirements on matters such as human rights, worker safety and environmental impact that producers, traders and retailers may be asked to meet, adopted voluntarily along the value chain.

facts.text: They arose as regulation of global business shifted from governments to private actors, with consumers holding companies to account.
They may be government-led, such as the USDA Organic label, or created by NGOs, such as FairTrade and Rainforest Alliance.
The FairTrade label aims to empower small producers mainly through a minimum price paid to them.
Many companies write their own standards instead, such as Starbucks' C.A.F.E. Practices.

definition.text: Partnerships of NGOs, companies, suppliers and governments that use voluntary, market-based approaches to make production of a particular product or sector more sustainable.

facts.text: They develop standards and issue certifications, and can also act as learning platforms.
Well-known examples include the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, the Forest Stewardship Council and the Better Cotton Initiative.
The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil awards a certified label to companies meeting criteria meant to limit palm oil's harm to people and the environment.

title: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures
article: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures

definition.text: An international task force whose recommendations tell investors how companies are managing the risks of climate change and how they are governed.

facts.text: It was set up in December 2015 by the G20 and the Financial Stability Board, and was chaired by Michael Bloomberg.
Its recommendations cover four areas: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets.
It was formed partly in response to the 2015 Paris Agreement, whose national pledges were criticized for lacking transparent disclosure standards.
Its aim is to give investors, lenders and insurers the information they need to assess and price climate-related risks and opportunities.
It is described as the main framework used globally for climate disclosure in ESG.
Ahead of COP26 in 2021, the UK became the first G20 country to require 1,300 of its largest companies to disclose in line with it.
At COP26 the IFRS announced the International Sustainability Standards Board, into which the TCFD will converge.

notes: International body created by the G20 and FSB, not a single NGO; seeded in this chapter.

definition.text: The two kinds of climate risk: physical risks from climate impacts such as extreme weather, and transition risks from the costs of moving to a lower-carbon society.

facts.text: For the financial sector, physical risks mean damage to property, infrastructure and land; transition risks come from changes in policy, technology and consumer behaviour.
Physical risks of climate change top the list of business concerns for US and EU firms.
Transition risk includes the financial effects of carbon pricing and stranded assets.
In 2015 Bank of England governor Mark Carney warned that meeting the 2 °C limit could leave most fossil fuel reserves as stranded assets.

definition.text: A set of standards that organizations use to measure and track their greenhouse gas emissions, the most common in greenhouse gas accounting.

facts.text: The World Resources Institute worked with companies to develop it, and its first version was published in September 2001.
It sorts an organization's emissions into Scope 1, 2 and 3; Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions from its activities.
For most businesses the great majority of emissions are Scope 3, coming from the wider supply chain rather than the site or purchased energy.
Scope 3 was estimated at 75% of all emissions reported to the Carbon Disclosure Project, varying widely by sector.
Scope 3 is hard to report accurately: in 2022 about 30% of US companies reported it, and double counting is a concern.
The Science Based Targets initiative and the TCFD both cite it, and the ISO 14064 standard is based on it.

title: Central banks and climate risk

definition.text: Green central banking: the idea that central banks should help reach net-zero targets and address climate change through their policies.

facts.text: By adjusting monetary policy and capital requirements, central banks can steer investment into green finance.
Bank of England governor Mark Carney backed the TCFD and called for financial firms to manage climate risk, notably through climate stress tests.
Many researchers argue that pursuing such goals raises serious questions about the legitimacy of independent central banks, which rarely have climate mandates.

contested_note: Researchers dispute whether independent central banks have the legitimacy to pursue climate goals.

definition.text: A flammable carbon or hydrocarbon material formed naturally in the Earth's crust from the buried remains of prehistoric organisms.

facts.text: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are burnt for heating, to power engines and to generate electricity; some are refined into kerosene, gasoline and diesel or turned into plastics and other petrochemicals.
Because they take millions of years to form, fossil fuels are non-renewable resources.
In 2023, 77% of world primary energy consumption and over 60% of electricity supply came from fossil fuels.
Over 70% of human greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 was CO2 from burning fossil fuels.

Burning them has negative externalities: CO2 that speeds climate change, plus particulates, smog and acid rain; air pollution from fossil fuels in 2018 was estimated to cost US$2.9 trillion, 3.3% of global GDP.

definition.text: The geological process by which buried dead organisms become coal, oil and gas.

facts.text: Plankton that died and sedimented in anoxic conditions began forming petroleum and natural gas by anaerobic decomposition; terrestrial plants tend to form coal and methane.
Burial under sediment brought heat and pressure that turned organic matter into kerogen and then liquid and gaseous hydrocarbons.
The energy released in combustion is still photosynthetic in origin.

title: Health effects of fossil fuel pollution

definition.text: The illness and premature death caused by inhaling particulates and other air pollution from burning fossil fuels.

facts.text: Effects include premature death, acute respiratory illness, aggravated asthma, chronic bronchitis and decreased lung function; the poor, very young, very old and those with respiratory disease are most at risk.
Global deaths from fossil-fuel air pollution were estimated at over 8 million in 2018 (nearly 1 in 5 deaths), 10.2 million in 2019 and 5.13 million excess deaths in 2023.
Fossil fuels cause the highest greenhouse gas emissions and are the most dangerous to health; modern renewables appear safer and cleaner.

definition.text: The impact of fossil fuel prices on inflation.

facts.text: Economists have pointed to energy prices as the main reason for high inflation in 2022; transport, food and shipping prices rise sharply when fossil fuel prices do.
Mark Zandi says fossil fuel prices have driven every big inflation episode since WWII.
Gernot Wagner argues commodities are volatile energy sources, whereas renewable technologies get relatively cheaper over time.
